newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia sees boost in trade of unlisted shares.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia sees boost in trade of unlisted shares.

text.p: Trade in unlisted shares of newly privatised Slovenian companies had soared in August despite official recommendations to hold on to the shares until their flotation, brokers said on Monday.
The Securities Market Agency recently warned citizens not to rush into selling the privatisation shares, saying stock prices tended to rise once the securities are listed.

"We have advised people not to sell shares before they are listed on the bourse, since experience has showed that prices rise when shares are listed," agency spokeswoman Jana Bogdanovski told Reuters.
But most Slovenians selling off their shares in a hurry are more interested in instant cash than a long-term investment, brokers said.

"Unlisted privatisation shares are mainly sold by people who need money as soon as possible and therefore do not care about profits they could make in the long run," said Karmen Cerar, a trader at the brokerage Poteza.

Trading company Mercator is one example of the many firms whose stock prices were buoyed by flotation. Mercator shares jumped to 4,000 tolars ($30) in April from 2,000 tolars after they were listed on the over-the-counter (OTC) market of the Ljubljana bourse.
On Monday Mercator closed at 3,645 tolars.
Brokers said shares of petrol trading company Petrol, drug producers Lek and Krka and brewery Lasko were currently among the most popular thanks to satisfactory business results.
The companies are due to be listed on the primary or OTC markets by the end of 1997.
Brokerages said they kept most of the unlisted privatisation shares they had acquired inactive, counting on greater profits once they have been listed.

In Slovenia's mass privatisation scheme after the demise of communist rule, each citizen received a privatisation voucher, worth between 100,000 tolars ($757) and 400,000 tolars, depending on the person's age.
More than 88 percent of Slovenians have already spent their privatisation vouchers on company shares, an opinion poll showed.
Slovenia's privatisation process involves 1,500 companies and is expected to be finished in mid-1997. Some 686 companies have already finished their privatisation.
